name: Fat grafting to chin

lead: Fat grafting moves your own fat from elsewhere on the body into the chin to add volume and projection. The result is a fuller, more defined chin, visible after treatment, using natural tissue instead of an implant or filler.

Fat is harvested, processed and reinjected. Part of it survives as living tissue and part is reabsorbed; transferred fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body, so weight gain or loss can affect results. Fat grafting is an established technique in general, with up to 50% resorption cited for breast augmentation, and the sources reviewed give no outcome data specific to the chin.

paras: It is a surgical procedure: fat is taken by liposuction, prepared and injected into the chin area. It is discussed as an alternative to implants, sliding genioplasty and injectable fillers, and sometimes done in more than one session as the fat settles.

Reported general risks include fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, asymmetry or lumpiness, infection and donor-site pain. Some grafted fat can be reabsorbed, so volume may change. It is performed by clinicians.

angle.text: Fat grafting builds out a small chin with your own fat, as an alternative to implants, genioplasty or fillers, and the added volume is visible after treatment. It is an established technique in general, with limited chin-specific data, and some of the fat can be reabsorbed.

lead: Fat grafting, also called fat transfer or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat from one body area to another. It involves harvesting fat, processing it and reinjecting it, and is used to add volume or smooth irregular areas [1]. Applied to the chin, it is one of several ways to change chin projection or contour, alongside implants, sliding genioplasty and injectable fillers [2].

Wikipedia reports that transferred fat can be partly reabsorbed, with up to 50% resorption cited for breast augmentation, and that weight gain or loss can affect results because grafted fat behaves like fat elsewhere in the body [1]. The pages reviewed for this entry do not give outcome data specific to the chin.
infobox: Fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes fat transfer as a surgical process in three stages and notes that facial rejuvenation has shifted from mainly removing skin and fat toward restoring volume to deflated facial compartments [1]. The article lists facial uses around the lower eyelid and mouth, and other uses such as breast reconstruction and scar treatment [1]. It does not list the chin specifically.

Wikipedia's article on chin augmentation describes implants of silicone or porous materials, sliding genioplasty in which a piece of jawbone is moved forward and fixed with plates, and temporary injectable fillers; it does not discuss fat grafting [2].

Wikipedia lists fat necrosis, swelling, bruising, hematoma, donor-site pain, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities and cannula injury as complications of fat transfer in general, and advises minimal handling of the graft to preserve survival [1].
